summary:
Project Tenacity is a browser tool for planning a walk on Mars before taking it. It borrows the way NASA's rover drivers work at JPL (sketch a drive, simulate it, validate it against rules) and gives the same loop to astronauts on foot at Gale Crater. It is built for astronauts and mission operations personnel, not for the general public.

The crew lays out a walk on real orbital imagery, or lets the tool find the easiest path over the terrain. Tenacity then simulates the walk step by step: time on every slope, oxygen, cooling water and battery, and how long it would take to get back to the refuge at any moment. Fifteen flight rules give one clear answer, GO or NO-GO, name the rule that decides, and show where on the map it bites.

More than 25 layers of NASA data (terrain, slope, shadow, minerals, subsurface water, rock chemistry, solar-storm forecasts and Curiosity's own photos of each stop) feed the same rules, so the map and the plan cannot disagree. A 3D flyover shows the ground before the crew walks it. Every number is labelled as measured, a NASA value, derived or assumed.
details:
WHO IT IS FOR

Tenacity is a professional tool, not a public outreach site. It is built for two kinds of user: astronauts, who plan the walk and then follow it, and mission operations personnel (flight controllers, EVA officers and planners), who have to clear it before the crew leaves. We chose completeness over simplicity, on purpose: a tool for trained users should keep every rule, number and source in view, not hide detail to look simpler. That is why the interface is dense, speaks in flight rules and NASA alert conventions, and shows its numbers and their sources instead of hiding them. A guided tour is built in so that judges and newcomers can find their way around.

WHAT IT DOES

Tenacity answers one question for a crew about to leave the airlock: is this walk safe, by how much, and what decides it?

1. Sketch. Load a ready-made walk, or click the map to add stations anywhere. Each leg can follow ground a rover has already driven, go in a straight line, or take the easiest path the terrain engine finds. Keep-out zones can be marked; paths go around them.

2. Simulate. The walk is simulated before it happens: pace and effort on every slope, oxygen, carbon dioxide, cooling water and battery, and the walk-home time from every point.

3. Validate. Fifteen flight rules are checked along the whole walk. Examples: the refuge must always be within 60 minutes at emergency pace, because that is how long a suit's backup supply lasts; ground steeper than 20 degrees may not be crossed in any direction; a solar eruption forecast to reach Mars blocks the walk. A rule whose data are missing or too old is shown as "not evaluated", never as a pass.

4. Understand. Click any point to read every layer there. Ask why a path was chosen: ground that cannot be crossed is shown in red, slow ground in yellow, and the straight line the path finder rejected is drawn. Fly along the route in 3D over real terrain and imagery, with Curiosity's own photograph of each station. Recordings of each of these steps in motion (sketching a walk, playback, the 3D flyover and the guided tour) are in the project repository: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity#in-motion

WHAT INSPIRED THE DESIGN

The design is modelled on RSVP (Robot Sequencing and Visualization Platform), the tool suite NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has used to plan surface operations on its Mars rovers and landers since 1997. Rover planners sketch a drive on the terrain, build it into a command sequence, simulate it, and check it before it is sent to Mars. Tenacity maps each part of that suite to a walk: the Activity list and sketching on the map follow MobSketch; the sequence table and console follow RoSE, the sequence editor; the walk simulation follows SSim, the surface simulation; and the terrain views, clocks and playback follow HyperDrive. Alert colours and layout rules follow NASA-STD-3001 and the crew-interface work at Johnson Space Center.

Source: https://www-robotics.jpl.nasa.gov/what-we-do/applications/user-interfaces/

HOW IT IS BUILT

A static web page: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript modules, with Leaflet for the 2D map and our own WebGL code for the 3D view. There is no server and no build step. The terrain engine runs in the browser in a web worker on a 5-million-cell elevation grid: slope, cast shadow for the time of day, line of sight to the refuge, a walk-home time field and least-time path finding. Data files are built from NASA's public services by Python scripts in the repository, so every file can be regenerated. Plans, notes and the history of changes are stored in the browser. 113 automated tests cover the simulation, the Mars clock, the terrain engine and the 3D maths.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

  • It treats a spacewalk the way mission operations treats a rover drive: a sequence that is simulated and checked against rules before anyone moves.
  • The layers are not pictures beside a planner. The same slope, shadow, sight-line and space-weather data drawn on the map are what the rules read.
  • It is honest about what is known. Every constant carries a tag (MEASURED, NASA VALUE, DERIVED, ASSUMED) and its source.
  • The interface follows NASA's display standard for alert colours and is built like a professional workstation: resizable docks, a guided tour, search, and a large mode for gloved hands.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Crew safety first: the limit that usually decides a walk is not oxygen but how far you can be from shelter if the suit fails. Mobility in a suit: slope limits, slow ground, loose ground. The environment: daylight for the season, cast shadow, radiation and solar storms. Working in pairs, with a pressurised rover as a refuge that can be re-parked. What the crew will see on arrival: rover photographs at the stations and a 3D view of the ground.

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

Walking speed and effort on Mars in a suit have never been measured; the model is extrapolated from Earth and Moon data. The elevation model is good for relative height, not absolute. Position error is not modelled. This is a first prototype for planning and training, not a certified flight product. The README lists every known limit.

INTENDED IMPACT

Rover planners simulate every drive before it happens. We want crews on foot to have the same habit and the same kind of tool.

USE OF AI

The team chose the challenge, set the concept, the requirements and the design direction, and reviewed and tested the result. Research was done in two ways: by hand (the team found and read primary NASA and JPL sources itself) and with AI tools (Perplexity, an AI search assistant, to locate and cross-check sources, and Claude, an AI coding assistant by Anthropic, for further background research). Most of the code and the data-building scripts were written with Claude under the team's direction. No AI-generated images, audio or video are part of the project: every picture is a screenshot or recording of the working tool.

Source code: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity - Project paper (PDF): https://yara-hue24.github.io/Project-Tenacity/docs/Tenacity-project-description.pdf
